university: University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill

documents.title: Student Generative AI Usage Guidance (UNC AI Committee)
documents.summary: The UNC Generative AI Committee, set up by the Provost and Deans, offers recommended syllabus language for instructors. It sets default principles (AI should help you think; you are responsible; use must be declared and documented), gives assignment-type guidance that mostly allows documented use, bans AI on exams unless the instructor permits, and leaves instructors free to override per assignment.
documents.stance_why: Stance is delegates: the cover note asks instructors to 'review and incorporate the recommended language in your syllabi, adapting them as you choose', and the guidelines apply 'Unless I provide other guidelines for an assignment or exam'. The document supplies a default framework but the instructor decides for the course; it is not a single university rule and has no named tiers.

units.why: The committee supplies 'recommended language' for instructors' syllabi; it is a template supplied by the institution, so P110 (sample syllabus language) rather than P56, which is about principles. Addressed to the institution's instructors via the cover note.
units.anchor: The UNC AI Committee has developed the following recommended language for student guidelines

units.why: States who made the guidance and how: 'the Provost and Deans created the UNC Generative AI Committee, with representatives from every academic unit'. That is a statement of origin and process, so P84.
units.anchor: the Provost and Deans created the UNC Generative AI Committee

units.why: The committee's premise that AI use is 'inevitable' acknowledges that AI cannot be prevented, which is why it is a limit-on-control statement (P82), not a rule.
units.anchor: society’s acceptance and use of generative AI is inevitable

units.why: 'Organizations will expect our students to have generative AI skills' is the career argument for learning AI use, so P44. The learning/productivity/creativity benefit in the same sentence is coded separately as P87.
units.anchor: Organizations will expect our students to have generative AI skills

units.why: Names benefits ('useful tools for learning, productivity, and creativity') without making a rule or a career claim, so P87.
units.anchor: will find them useful tools for learning, productivity, and creativity

units.why: The guiding principle that AI 'should help you think. Not think for you' says students stay the primary thinker, so P32. It is stated as a philosophy (informs).
units.anchor: “AI should help you think. Not think for you.”

units.why: Asks instructors to put the language into syllabi ('Please review and incorporate ... in your syllabi'), a request rather than a mandate, hence should. Closest type is P09 (AI statement in the syllabus).
units.anchor: Please review and incorporate the recommended language in your syllabi
units.fit_note: Phrased as a request to adopt the committee's language and adapt it, not a requirement to have a statement.

units.why: Recommends covering the guidelines on 'the first day of class', i.e. going over the rules with students beyond printing them, so P66 (explain and discuss the rules).
units.anchor: It is also recommended that you cover them on the first day of class.
units.fit_note: Only says to cover the guidelines on day one; no mention of reasons or discussion.

units.why: The instructor 'can have different guidelines for a specific assignment or exam', so the rule is set per assignment by the instructor: P04.
units.anchor: as the course instructor you can have different guidelines for a specific assignment or exam

units.why: Says the guidelines will 'continue to evolve' and (next sentence) invites feedback: a revisit statement, P54.
units.anchor: we expect these guidelines to continue to evolve

units.why: Names a contact person and the academic-unit representatives for questions and feedback on the guidelines, i.e. who owns and answers for the policy: P80.
units.anchor: if you have any questions or feedback, please contact Mark McNeilly
units.fit_note: A contact for questions and feedback, not an enforcement or exception office.

units.why: Lists as a limitation that 'how output is arrived at is not clear', which is part of why users must scrutinize output; nearest type is P31.
units.anchor: how output is arrived at is not clear
units.fit_note: Opacity of AI processes rather than wrongness of output.

units.why: States AI output 'may also be inaccurate or entirely fabricated', the core of P31.
units.anchor: may also be inaccurate or entirely fabricated, even if it appears reliable or factual

units.why: Says output 'may reflect biases that should be acknowledged', a bias concern with an obligation to acknowledge it, so P53.
units.anchor: may reflect biases that should be acknowledged

units.why: 'AI evokes a range of intellectual property concerns; sourcing and ownership of information is unclear' raises ownership of AI output, which is P52.
units.anchor: AI evokes a range of intellectual property concerns

units.why: Notes that the guidelines cover AI features built into everyday applications ('increasingly, generative AI capabilities will be integrated with everyday applications'), the embedded-AI scope of P07.
units.anchor: generative AI capabilities will be integrated with everyday applications
units.fit_note: A factual note on scope; no instruction about editors, IDEs or disabling features.

units.why: The principle's explanation lets students 'Use these tools to give you ideas, perform research ... and analyze problems', a permission for idea generation, so P15.
units.anchor: Use these tools to give you ideas, perform research
units.fit_note: Also permits research and analyzing problems, not only brainstorming.

units.why: 'Do not use them to do your work for you ... copy & paste the response as your answer' forbids having AI produce the submitted work: P19.
units.anchor: do not enter an assignment question into ChatGPT and copy & paste the response

units.why: Directs students to engage 'critically evaluating AI-generated outputs and considering potential biases', i.e. verify and evaluate output: P31.
units.anchor: critically evaluating AI-generated outputs and considering potential biases, limitations, and ethical implications

units.why: A general call to 'Utilize AI technologies ethically' naming privacy, confidentiality and IP without specific instructions, so P116.
units.anchor: Utilize AI technologies ethically, respecting privacy, confidentiality, and intellectual property rights.
units.fit_note: Names privacy, confidentiality and IP as areas but gives no concrete rule.

units.why: Requires data used with AI to be obtained and shared 'in compliance with relevant regulations', a compliance-with-law rule: P77.
units.anchor: obtained and shared responsibly and in compliance with relevant regulations

units.why: 'You are 100% responsible for your final product' makes students own what they submit: P29.
units.anchor: You are 100% responsible for your final product.

units.why: Tells students to delete AI content they cannot verify ('If you cannot verify it as factual, you should delete it'), a verify-output rule: P31.
units.anchor: If you cannot verify it as factual, you should delete it.

units.why: 'The use of any AI ... must be declared in your submission and explained' is a mandatory disclosure with each submission: P24.
units.anchor: must be declared in your submission and explained

units.why: Puts the duty on students to find out which rules apply ('It is your responsibility to ensure you are following the correct guidelines'), given instructors may set assignment-specific rules: P78.
units.anchor: It is your responsibility to ensure you are following the correct guidelines.

units.why: Students should not enter confidential or personal data (the text gives One Card details as an example) into AI tools: protect personal data, P50.
units.anchor: Data that are confidential or personal should not be entered into generative AI tools.

units.why: Violating the guidelines 'may be a reportable violation to the UNC Honor Court', which routes misuse to the integrity process: P36.
units.anchor: may be a reportable violation to the UNC Honor Court

units.why: For writing and presentations 'you may submit material that contains AI-generated content ... if this use is properly documented'; permission to submit AI-generated material on condition of documentation matches P16 (the type name mentions code but the definition covers use of AI-generated work under conditions).
units.anchor: you may submit material that contains AI-generated content, or is based on
units.fit_note: Applies to writing and presentation material, not code.

units.why: 'Your documentation must make the process transparent' requires disclosure of how AI was used in writing assignments: P24.
units.anchor: Your documentation must make the process transparent

units.why: For multimedia assignments students may submit AI-generated images, audio, music or video if documented, which is the images-and-graphics permission P106.
units.anchor: This may include the generation of images, audio, music, video, etc.
units.fit_note: Covers audio, music and video as well as images.

units.why: Lists math, statistical and data analysis and says 'Generative AI can be used for these purposes': the data-analysis permission P89.
units.anchor: Generative AI can be used for these purposes
units.fit_note: Verification condition is coded separately.

units.why: AI output in analysis 'must be verified via your own mathematical calculations and proof of work', a verification duty: P31.
units.anchor: the output must be verified via your own mathematical calculations and proof of work provided
units.fit_note: Also requires proof of the verification work in the assignment.

units.why: Permits AI to 'analyze readings' as an aid to understanding material, closest to P12 (AI as a tutor for understanding), with the proviso in the next sentence.
units.anchor: Generative AI can be used to analyze readings.
units.fit_note: Permission is to analyze assigned readings, and it is conditioned on also doing the readings.

units.why: Says AI analysis 'is not a substitute for reading the works themselves', so AI must not replace the student's own engagement; P32 fits best.
units.anchor: Generative AI analysis is not a substitute for reading the works themselves.
units.fit_note: Specific to readings: students must do the readings themselves.

units.why: 'do not generate responses to readings using AI' unless the instructor allows is a ban on AI producing submitted responses: P19.
units.anchor: Unless I specifically allow it, do not generate responses to readings using AI.

units.why: 'you must account for and document your use' of AI in research is mandatory disclosure: P24.
units.anchor: you must account for and document your use

units.why: Lists research uses of AI (search assistance, source evaluation, summaries) as possibilities, which is the literature-and-sources permission P104.
units.anchor: topic brainstorming, search assistance, source evaluation, and summaries and source documentation

units.why: 'Track your use of AI throughout these stages, and then document this assistance' requires keeping a record of AI use and submitting it: P26.
units.anchor: Track your use of AI throughout these stages

units.why: AI-generated material 'should also be documented in your citations': citing AI use in the submission, P24.
units.anchor: Any material generated through AI in your projects should also be documented in your citations.

units.why: For simulations students 'may use AI tools for advice or brainstorming': P15.
units.anchor: you may use AI tools for advice or brainstorming

units.why: Bars using AI in simulations to 'find cheats or other unfair advantages'. This is a specific prohibition on exploiting a simulation, which none of the types P19-P23 describes.
units.anchor: It should not, however, be used to find cheats or other unfair advantages.
units.uncovered_note: In simulation assignments, AI must not be used to find cheats or unfair advantages in the simulation.

units.why: Sets AI rules for group work by tying them to the assignment type ('a group written assignment will use the guidelines for written assignments'): P127.
units.anchor: Group work guidelines are based on the type of assignment above

units.why: Leaves AI use in in-class activities to instructions from the instructor ('will be provided by me'), so the rule is set per activity: P04.
units.anchor: Instructions on the appropriate use of AI for in-class activities will be provided by me.

units.why: For written and oral exams AI 'is prohibited' unless the instructor explicitly permits: P22. The Honor Court consequence is a further clause of the same sentence.
units.anchor: Unless I explicitly grant permission, the utilization of AI tools is prohibited

units.why: Where exam AI is permitted, students 'are required to adhere to the guidelines concerning AI citation, verification, and clarity': disclosure duty carried into exams, P24.
units.anchor: you are required to adhere to the guidelines concerning AI citation, verification, and clarity
units.fit_note: Also requires verification and clarity, not just citation.

units.why: 'Generative AI may invent both facts and sources ... Verification is your responsibility': verify AI output because it is often wrong, P31.
units.anchor: Verification is your responsibility

units.why: Students must check facts, quotes, arguments and logic 'and document what you did to validate your material': a verification duty with documentation, P31.
units.anchor: document what you did to validate your material
units.fit_note: Adds a duty to document the validation steps.

units.why: When AI names a source, students must 'find and attribute the original source of the idea' and give a working link, a check on AI-supplied sources (the text warns AI 'tends to invent sources'). P31 is nearest.
units.anchor: find and attribute the original source of the idea
units.fit_note: Requires attributing the original source with location and link, beyond verifying output.

units.why: Content whose source cannot be located must be deleted, a verify-or-remove rule: P31.
units.anchor: If you are not able to locate the source, delete that content.

units.why: Requires a 'work statement' accompanying major projects explaining AI use: disclosure with each submission, P24.
units.anchor: Document the process by explaining how you used generative AI in a work statement

units.why: Students must 'include an appropriate version of the below statements' (attesting either no AI use or AI use in listed ways) with each project: disclosure with each submission, P24.
units.anchor: As you submit a project, develop, and include an appropriate version of the below statements:
units.fit_note: Uses a standard attestation either way, not free-form disclosure.

units.why: A required form records, for each use, the tool used (e.g. ChatGPT-4), how the output was edited and a conversation link; that is detail on tool and output, so P25 rather than generic P24.
units.anchor: You must then use the following form to document your usage.
units.fit_note: Also asks how the output was edited and the stage of work (topic selection, drafting, polishing, etc.).

units.why: Clarifies that citing an AI is 'not a valid source for facts, only for the output itself', so facts must still be traced to real sources; closest to P31.
units.anchor: such attribution is not a valid source for facts, only for the output itself.
units.fit_note: Clarifies what an AI citation does and does not establish.

units.why: The committee discloses that 'ChatGPT was used in the development of these guidelines', a disclosure of AI-made course/policy material: P48.
units.anchor: ChatGPT was used in the development of these guidelines
units.fit_note: A disclosure about a policy document, not about course materials.

units.why: Names Sentient Syllabus as a source of ideas, part of how the guidance was made: P84.
units.anchor: Sentient Syllabus was a resource for a number of the ideas

documents.title: Student Use Guidelines for Generative AI
tiers: Template A: no generative AI of any kind in the course (violations referred to the Honor System)
Template B: a listed set of permitted uses (e.g. topic selection, brainstorming, research, drafting, polishing), with attribution and a usage form
documents.summary: The College of Arts & Sciences adapts the university committee's guidance into student guidelines and an instructor cover note. It sets principles (AI should help you think; student is 100% responsible; use must be declared; no confidential data), and tells instructors to pick one of two syllabus statements: a full ban or a list of permitted uses with verification and a documentation form.
documents.stance_why: Stance is delegates: principle 2 says 'The rules for use of AI in particular courses are to be determined by the course instructor', and instructors are told to specify either a full ban or a list of permitted uses. The college offers two templates (tiers) and sets no stance of its own.

units.why: Says how the college text was made: 'the College AI Committee was convened to tailor these recommendations' from the university committee's guidance, a process statement: P84.
units.anchor: the College AI Committee was convened to tailor these recommendations

units.why: Treats AI use as 'inevitable', an acknowledgement that it cannot be stopped: P82.
units.anchor: society’s acceptance and use of generative AI is inevitable

units.why: 'Organizations will expect our students to have skills in using AI tools' is the professional-skill argument, P44.
units.anchor: Organizations will expect our students to have skills in using AI tools

units.why: States benefits (learning, productivity, creativity) without a rule: P87.
units.anchor: will find them useful for learning, productivity, and creativity

units.why: The guiding philosophy 'AI should help you think, not think for you' keeps the student as the thinker: P32.
units.anchor: “AI should help you think, not think for you.”

units.why: 'strongly recommended that you include a statement on your syllabus indicating which uses ... are permitted': the college urges, but does not require, an AI statement in every syllabus, so P09 with should.
units.anchor: It is strongly recommended that you include a statement on your syllabus

units.why: The parenthetical says permitted uses 'may vary from assignment to assignment', so the instructor sets the rule per assignment: P04.
units.anchor: which may vary from assignment to assignment

units.why: Gives a list of 'Categories of possible permitted use' (topic selection through polishing) for instructors to choose from per course; a set of named categories of use, so P05.
units.anchor: topic selection, brainstorming and idea generation, research, source validation, outlining and planning, drafting
units.fit_note: Categories of use rather than levels of permission; instructors pick which are allowed.

units.why: 'we expect these guidelines to continue to evolve' and feedback is invited: P54.
units.anchor: we expect these guidelines to continue to evolve

units.why: Names the college AI mailbox as the contact for questions and feedback, an owner of the guidelines: P80.
units.anchor: please contact CAS.AI@unc.edu.
units.fit_note: A contact point for questions and feedback, not enforcement or exceptions.

units.why: Describes what generative AI is ('can produce text, images, and other media'), setting the scope of the guidelines: P61.
units.anchor: ChatGPT and other generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) can produce text, images, and other media.

units.why: General call: tools 'must be used appropriately and ethically' and users 'must understand their limitations', with no specific content: P116.
units.anchor: they must be used appropriately and ethically, and you must understand their limitations

units.why: Students are 'responsible for the final product of your work' regardless of AI use: P29.
units.anchor: you are responsible for the final product of your work

units.why: Warns users take responsibility for AI content they 'do not fully understand', pointing to the need to understand what they submit; nearest type P30.
units.anchor: taking on responsibility for procedures and content that they do not fully understand
units.fit_note: A risk statement about not understanding AI procedures, not an explicit duty to explain every line.

units.why: Output 'may be inaccurate or entirely fabricated' (with fabricated journal articles as an example): P31.
units.anchor: AI-generated output may be inaccurate or entirely fabricated, even if it appears reliable or factual

units.why: Students who use AI must 'take responsibility for keeping themselves informed about relevant developments': a duty to stay informed, P102.
units.anchor: students who use AI to take responsibility for keeping themselves informed about relevant developments

units.why: Says AI norms 'vary substantially depending on the discipline, course, instructor, and assignment': the rule is set per instructor and assignment, P04.
units.anchor: may vary substantially depending on the discipline, course, instructor, and assignment

units.why: Names bias in AI output ('may reflect biases and other inadequacies in that data'): P53.
units.anchor: may reflect biases and other inadequacies in that data

units.why: Raises ownership of AI output and whether it counts as a published resource: P52.
units.anchor: Generative AI raises a range of intellectual property concerns regarding the ownership of its output

units.why: Warns AI may produce content that infringes copyright: a copyright risk, P52.
units.anchor: may produce content that infringes on others’ intellectual property or copyright-protected works

units.why: Warns AI content can lead to 'allegations of plagiarism or other forms of academic dishonesty' against students: unintentional plagiarism risk, P120.
units.anchor: content that leads to allegations of plagiarism or other forms of academic dishonesty

units.why: Explains that anything entered into a public AI tool 'is effectively being shared publicly': a data-privacy warning, P50.
units.anchor: Any information that is entered into a public AI tool such as ChatGPT

units.why: 'Violation of these principles may result in an Honor System referral' ties misuse to the integrity process: P36.
units.anchor: Violation of these principles may result in an Honor System referral.

units.why: 'AI tools should not be used to do your work for you ... never acceptable ... copy/paste the response as your answer': P19.
units.anchor: never acceptable for you to enter an essay prompt or problem set question into ChatGPT

units.why: Lists uses that may be appropriate 'Depending on the course and assignment' (brainstorm, research, analyze, images, improve writing); brainstorming is the lead use, so P15.
units.anchor: AI tools can appropriately be used to help you brainstorm, perform research, analyze problems
units.fit_note: Also lists research, analysis, images and writing improvement, and is conditional on the course.

units.why: 'The rules for use of AI in particular courses are to be determined by the course instructor' hands the decision to instructors: P04.
units.anchor: for use of AI in particular courses are to be determined by the course

units.why: Students with questions about permitted AI use 'should consult me': ask the instructor when unsure, P10.
units.anchor: you should consult me for clarification and guidance

units.why: 'you should not assume that a particular use ... acceptable in one academic context will also be acceptable in other contexts': a course's rule does not carry over, P11.
units.anchor: you should not assume that a particular use of AI tools that was acceptable

units.why: 'You are 100% responsible for the work that you submit': P29.
units.anchor: You are 100% responsible for the work that you submit.

units.why: Mistakes the student relies on from AI are 'your mistake': owning what you submit, P29.
units.anchor: If an AI tool makes a mistake, and you rely on it

units.why: Students must research doubtful AI statements and not include what they 'cannot independently verify': verify AI output, P31.
units.anchor: if you cannot independently verify its accuracy, you should not rely on it

units.why: AI use 'must be declared in your submission and explained': disclosure with each submission, P24.
units.anchor: must be declared in your submission and explained.

units.why: Students should not enter confidential or personal data into public AI tools: P50.
units.anchor: Data that are confidential or personal should not be entered into public generative AI tools.

units.why: 'Instructors should specify details of AI Use Policies for the particular course': an AI statement in the course, P09.
units.anchor: Instructors should specify details of AI Use Policies for the particular course

units.why: Offers instructors template wording banning AI entirely ('not permitted in this course'). It is an option the instructor may adopt, so the unit stance is prohibit but the document itself does not impose it; P01 matches the content.
units.anchor: Use of generative AI tools of any kind is not permitted in this course.
units.fit_note: A template option instructors may choose, not a default imposed by the college.

units.why: In the no-AI template, any use 'will be considered an instance of academic dishonesty and will be referred to the Honor System': misuse as misconduct, P36.
units.anchor: Any use of these tools will be considered an instance of academic dishonesty

units.why: The second template says only 'The following uses ... are permitted', a closed list of tasks chosen by the instructor: P107 (limit AI to listed tasks).
units.anchor: The following uses of generative AI tools are permitted in this course:
units.fit_note: A template for an instructor-chosen list of permitted uses.

units.why: Where AI use is permitted, 'Generative AI may fabricate both claims and sources' and 'Verification is your responsibility': P31.
units.anchor: Verification is your responsibility.

units.why: Students must 'independently verify the claims, quotations, sources, and reasoning' and document the steps: verify AI output, P31.
units.anchor: document the steps you took to perform this verification
units.fit_note: Adds a duty to document the verification steps.

units.why: 'You must attribute any use ... of words or ideas that are not originally your own' is a citation duty: P24.
units.anchor: You must attribute any use in your work of words or ideas

units.why: When AI names a source students 'must find and attribute the original source' and give its location: checking AI-given sources, P31.
units.anchor: you must find and attribute the original source of the words or ideas
units.fit_note: Requires attributing the original source with location, beyond verifying output.

units.why: Content whose source cannot be located should not be used: verify-or-omit, P31.
units.anchor: you should not make use of the content.

units.why: A 'work statement' explaining how AI was used must accompany major projects: P24.
units.anchor: You must document the process by explaining how you used generative AI

units.why: Silence is 'treated as an attestation that you did not use AI tools', so undisclosed use becomes a false attestation: nondisclosure matters for integrity, P28.
units.anchor: treated as an attestation that you did not use AI tools
units.fit_note: No explicit penalty; the consequence is that no statement counts as a no-AI attestation.

units.why: Students who used AI are asked to include a standard statement ('I attest that this project made use of AI in the following ways'): P24.
units.anchor: please include the following statement:
units.fit_note: Standard attestation wording.

units.why: The required form lists tool used (e.g. ChatGPT-4), how the output was edited and a conversation link, which is tool-and-output detail: P25.
units.anchor: You must then use the following form to document your usage.
units.fit_note: Also asks which stage of work the AI was used for.

units.why: An AI attribution is 'not a valid source for facts, only for the output itself', so facts must still be verified: P31.
units.anchor: such attribution is not a valid source for facts, only for the output itself.
units.fit_note: Clarifies what an AI citation does and does not establish.

units.why: The college discloses that 'ChatGPT was used in the development of these guidelines': disclosure of AI-made policy material, P48.
units.anchor: ChatGPT was used in the development of these guidelines
units.fit_note: A disclosure about a policy document, not course materials.

documents.title: Guidance on Generative AI Use (Graduate School Handbook)
documents.summary: The Graduate School Handbook page asks graduate programs to embrace the university committee's philosophy that humans are responsible for AI and that AI should help you think. It lets programs set their own thesis and exam rules, applies campus student and teaching guidance to graduate students and TAs, and lists discussion topics (disclosure, appendices, journal and funder rules, IP, data leakage) for students and advisors.
documents.stance_why: Stance is delegates: the Board 'encourages graduate programs to embrace the philosophy', says 'Individual graduate programs may establish guidelines specific to their thesis and comprehensive exams', and frames research use as a topic to 'be discussed with supervisors, advisors'. It sets no ban or permission itself.

units.why: The Board 'encourages graduate programs to embrace the philosophy' that humans are responsible for AI use and AI should help you think; an institution-level principle for programs, P56.
units.anchor: encourages graduate programs to embrace the philosophy
units.fit_note: Addressed to programs; it encourages adopting the principle, not a rule for students.

units.why: Says AI 'can be a productive tool and foster new directions and perspectives' for teaching and research: a benefit statement, P87.
units.anchor: can be a productive tool and foster new directions and perspectives

units.why: Users 'should take full responsibility for their use of AI and any research that might result': owning what one produces, P29.
units.anchor: should take full responsibility for their use of AI and any research

units.why: Programs 'may establish guidelines specific to their thesis and comprehensive exams': units may set their own rules, P85.
units.anchor: Individual graduate programs may establish guidelines specific to their thesis and comprehensive exams

units.why: Where a program encourages AI, campus student-use guidance 'should also apply to graduate students in their own classes and research': it sets the scope of the university framework for graduate students, P56.
units.anchor: guidance developed for the campus related to student use should also apply to graduate students
units.fit_note: Scope statement extending campus guidance to graduate students.

units.why: Reminds students they 'are always subject to the UNC Student Code of Conduct', i.e. AI use falls under existing university policy: P77.
units.anchor: they are always subject to the UNC Student Code of Conduct

units.why: Campus teaching-use guidance 'should also apply to instructors, including teaching assistants', extending the institutional framework to TAs: P56.
units.anchor: should also apply to instructors, including teaching assistants
units.fit_note: Scope statement for instructors and TAs.

units.why: Programs can encourage TAs to connect with supervisors so that 'the supervisor supports the TA using AI in their own grading/teaching work': TA AI use in teaching depends on supervisor support, nearest P59.
units.anchor: the supervisor supports the TA using AI in their own grading/teaching work
units.fit_note: Requires supervisor support for TA AI use in grading and teaching and compliance of student use with class guidelines.

units.why: Programs 'should share these resources and guidance' with TAs, directing them to the guidance: P115.
units.anchor: Graduate programs should share these resources and guidance with any graduate students serving as TAs.

units.why: AI use in research and writing 'should be discussed with supervisors, advisors, committee members': an AI rule for graduate research, P62.
units.anchor: should be discussed with supervisors, advisors, committee members, and any other associated individuals
units.fit_note: A duty to discuss AI use with advisors rather than deferring to venue rules.

units.why: Warns AI use 'might lead to data leakage' and permanence of unverified data: a data-protection warning, P50.
units.anchor: use of AI might lead to data leakage and proliferation, permanence, and widespread availability

units.why: Lists the order of writing, editing and using AI tools as a topic students and advisors should discuss; it touches the sequencing in P90 but is only a discussion topic.
units.anchor: Order of writing and editing and using these tools
units.fit_note: Only a topic for discussion, not a rule that students draft before using AI.

units.why: Students and advisors should discuss journal and granting-agency AI policies, i.e. defer to venue and funder rules: P62.
units.anchor: appropriate journal policies and granting agency policies relevant to the field of study

units.why: Raises that journals 'may disallow submission of material that has been previously submitted to AI sites' as previously published: a copyright and ownership concern, P52.
units.anchor: certain journals may disallow submission of material that has been previously submitted to AI sites

units.why: Lists research stages (design, drafting, data analysis, media) that students should discuss with advisors regarding AI: governing AI in research, P62.
units.anchor: Discuss methods/development of research design, drafts and writing generation and editing

units.why: Lists 'Citations and/or a statement disclosing specific uses of AI' as something to settle for research outputs: disclosure with the work, P24.
units.anchor: Citations and/or a statement disclosing specific uses of AI
units.fit_note: A discussion topic for research products rather than a fixed requirement.

units.why: Suggests an appendix documenting 'any exchanges (input or output ...) using AI', i.e. keeping and submitting the AI exchanges: P26.
units.anchor: Include appendix documenting any exchanges (input or output of materials, texts, or data) using AI
units.fit_note: A discussion topic, not a fixed requirement.

units.why: Suggests a methods section 'explaining the use of AI and its impact on research/products', a disclosure inside the work: P24.
